 These eight states still tax Social Security benefits in 2026, though each applies its own income limits and exemptions
 1 / 10 List slides Which states tax Social Security benefits in 2026? List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 20, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The list of states that tax Social Security keeps getting shorter. More than a dozen collected income tax on at least part of a retiree's benefits at the start of the decade. Eight still do in 2026, after West Virginia finished a multiyear phase-out that wipes the tax from its books. Kansas, Missouri and Nebraska all stopped taxing benefits beginning with the 2024 tax year.
 The eight that remain are Colorado, Connecticut, Minnesota, Montana, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Utah and Vermont. None of them taxes benefits the way the federal government does, and none taxes the full benefit for every retiree. Each has built its own mix of income thresholds, age rules, subtractions or credits that spares lower- and middle-income households while still collecting from retirees who have substantial pension, investment or retirement-account income stacked on top of their monthly checks.
 That design matters more than the label. Appearing on this list does not make a state expensive to retire in. Colorado exempts benefits outright once a resident turns 65. New Mexico's exemption reaches single filers earning up to $100,000. Montana has no general sales tax, which offsets some of what it collects on benefits. Several states that leave Social Security alone recover the money elsewhere — through high property taxes, broad sales taxes, or full taxation of pensions and 401(k) withdrawals. Those costs hit a fixed income just as hard.
 The federal rules sit underneath all of it. Up to 85% of a benefit is already taxable at the federal level once combined income passes certain levels, and some states simply adopt that calculation instead of writing their own. Others treat the federal number as a starting point and then apply their own adjustments, which is why two retirees with identical benefits can owe different amounts in neighboring states.
 What follows is a state-by-state breakdown of how each of the eight treats Social Security income in 2026 — the exemption cutoffs, the age requirements, the credits, and the wider tax picture that decides whether a retiree there owes anything at all.
 Colorado exempts Social Security fully at age 65 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Colorado does not tax Social Security benefits for residents age 65 and older. The deduction covers the entire federally taxable portion of those benefits with no income ceiling, which removes most of the state's retired population from the tax. The unlimited version of that deduction took effect with the 2022 tax year.
 The rule is unusual among the eight states because it turns on age rather than earnings. A 68-year-old with a large pension and a substantial brokerage account claims the same full deduction as a 68-year-old living on benefits alone. There is no phase-out to calculate and no threshold to track from one year to the next.
 Younger recipients are the group still exposed. People drawing Social Security disability or survivor payments before 65, along with early retirees who claimed at 62, do not automatically get the full deduction. Colorado's subtraction for retirement income at those ages is narrower and carries a dollar cap, and anything above the cap flows into state taxable income.
 Colorado applies a single flat rate to taxable income rather than graduated brackets. The state therefore does not scale what it collects on benefits to a retiree's overall income, the way the combined-income states do. The deduction either covers the benefit or it does not.
 The result is a state that taxes Social Security on paper and exempts nearly everyone who collects it. For anyone past 65, Colorado's treatment matches that of a state with no Social Security tax at all.
 The bigger budget variable in Colorado is cost of living. Housing prices in the Denver metro area and in mountain resort towns sit well above national averages. Property taxes run low by comparison — Colorado's effective residential rates are among the lowest in the country — which eases the picture for homeowners on fixed incomes. Residents still in their late 50s or early 60s should plan for state tax on part of their benefits until the year they turn 65.
 Connecticut shields most retirees under income caps 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Connecticut fully exempts Social Security benefits from state income tax for single filers with federal adjusted gross income below $75,000 and for joint filers below $100,000. Retirees under those limits still report the benefits on a federal return, but Connecticut collects nothing on them.
 Crossing a threshold does not expose the whole benefit. A partial exemption applies above the caps, so only a portion of the federally taxable amount reaches the state return. That design softens the edge for a household that clears the limit by a few thousand dollars.
 The exemption covers most retirees in practice. A household whose monthly checks make up the bulk of its income rarely approaches $75,000 in adjusted gross income, since the caps sit well above typical benefit levels. The filers who end up owing tend to be those layering a pension, required minimum distributions, rental income or investment gains on top of Social Security.
 Because the test runs on federal adjusted gross income, choices made during the year decide the outcome. The timing of an IRA withdrawal, a Roth conversion or the sale of appreciated stock can lift a return over the line, and the same transaction split across two tax years may not. Retirees sitting close to the cutoff have more control here than the flat numbers suggest.
 The exemption also sits inside a heavy overall tax climate. Connecticut runs a graduated income tax and high property taxes, with the sharpest costs concentrated in Fairfield County and the commuter towns within reach of New York City. A retiree comparing states on total cost may find those bills outweigh the value of untaxed benefits.
 Connecticut has revisited its treatment of retirement income across recent legislative sessions, adjusting exemptions for pension and annuity income alongside the Social Security rules. The state Department of Revenue Services publishes the governing thresholds and worksheets for each tax year, and those are the figures to check before filing rather than the prior year's.
 Minnesota taxes Social Security only if the federal government does 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Minnesota taxes Social Security benefits only to the extent the federal government does. Benefits that are not taxable on a federal return are not taxable in Minnesota, so a retiree whose combined income falls below the federal thresholds owes the state nothing on those benefits.
 Filers above that line get a second layer that works in their favor. Minnesota allows a subtraction for Social Security income that reduces, and often erases, the taxable amount carried over from the federal return. The subtraction depends on filing status and income, and it shrinks as income rises. Two households collecting identical monthly checks can therefore owe very different amounts to the state.
 The benefit itself is rarely the variable. What matters is everything stacked alongside it — a pension, required minimum distributions from an IRA or 401(k), dividends, rental income, part-time wages. Those dollars lift the combined income figure behind the federal calculation and then push a filer deeper into the phase-out range for the state subtraction. A retiree living on benefits alone rarely trips either trigger.
 Repeal comes up regularly at the Capitol in St. Paul. Lawmakers have introduced proposals to scrap the tax outright, in part because neighboring states have already dropped theirs. The 2023 tax law widened the subtraction instead of ending the tax. That conformity-plus-subtraction structure still governs the 2026 tax year.
 The rest of the state's tax picture deserves a look from anyone running retirement numbers. Minnesota's income tax brackets top out higher than those in most states, and they apply to pension income and retirement-account withdrawals with no blanket exclusion for retirement income. Property taxes vary sharply between Hennepin and Ramsey counties and rural townships in the north. The state also runs a property tax refund, known as the homestead credit refund, that returns money to qualifying homeowners based on income and tax paid. For a household on a fixed income, that refund can be worth more than the Social Security subtraction.
 Montana applies a modified federal formula to benefits 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Montana starts from the federal calculation and then adjusts it. The state uses its own worksheet, which takes the federally taxable share of a retiree's Social Security and applies Montana-specific modifications, so the amount subject to state tax can land above or below the federal figure.
 Combined income drives the result, not the size of the monthly check. A retiree living on Social Security alone generally sees little or none of it taxed, because the federal calculation feeding the state worksheet produces a small taxable share at low income levels. Add a pension, required minimum distributions from a 401(k) or IRA, part-time wages or dividends, and a larger portion of the benefit becomes taxable on both returns.
 That structure makes Montana harder to plan around than states using a flat dollar cutoff. No single income figure separates taxable benefits from exempt ones. The answer depends on the full return, and because the state calculation builds on the federal one, a change in federal taxability flows through to what Montana collects.
 Montana charges no general statewide sales tax, which changes the math for anyone comparing total cost rather than one line item. A retiree who spends heavily on goods and services avoids a charge that other states collect at the register, and that savings can outweigh what the state takes from a partially taxable benefit.
 Property taxes vary sharply by county, and valuations in resort areas such as the Flathead and Gallatin valleys have risen faster than in the eastern part of the state. Montana offers an elderly homeowner and renter credit, which can return part of what a qualifying low-income household pays in property tax or rent.
 Montana also taxes most other retirement income, including private pensions and traditional retirement-account withdrawals. Social Security sits inside a broader state income tax picture rather than standing as an isolated charge. Two households collecting identical benefits can owe different amounts in Montana depending on everything else reported on the return.
 New Mexico exempts benefits for nearly all retirees 
 Illustration: Quartz
 New Mexico exempts Social Security benefits from state income tax for single filers with adjusted gross income below $100,000 and joint filers below $150,000. Those cutoffs sit high enough that most retired households in the state owe nothing on their benefits.
 The exemption dates to a tax package the Legislature passed in 2022 and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed. New Mexico had taxed benefits for most recipients before that. The change arrived in a single session instead of the multi-year phase-outs other states have used to retire the tax.
 Retirees above the cap lose the exemption and report their benefits as ordinary income under New Mexico's graduated rate schedule. That group skews toward households drawing a sizable pension, large required minimum distributions, or investment income stacked on top of their benefits. A couple living on Social Security plus modest savings rarely reaches the threshold.
 The tradeoff sits elsewhere in the tax code. New Mexico levies a gross receipts tax rather than a conventional sales tax, and it reaches further — covering many services, including professional fees and repair work, that go untaxed in other states. Rates vary by city and county. The cost lands on routine spending rather than on retirement income.
 Property taxes run low by national standards, which matters for retirees who own their homes outright and live on a fixed monthly income. The state also lets qualifying homeowners age 65 and older whose income falls under a set limit freeze the assessed value of a primary residence. That protects long-term owners from rising valuations in markets like Santa Fe and Albuquerque.
 The result is a system that collects little from retirement income and more from consumption. Retirees who own a home and spend modestly pay less in total state and local tax than New Mexico's place on this list suggests.
 Rhode Island ties its exemption to retirement age and income 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Rhode Island exempts Social Security benefits only for residents who pass two separate tests. They must have reached full retirement age under federal rules, and their federal adjusted gross income must fall below a state limit indexed to inflation. Fail either test and part of the benefit stays taxable.
 The age test is what separates Rhode Island from the other seven states on this list. Full retirement age is 66 for people born between 1943 and 1954 and 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, with a sliding scale in between. Someone who filed early at 62 collects benefits for several years before the exemption becomes available. Disability and survivor beneficiaries who have not reached full retirement age fall outside it on the same grounds.
 The income cutoffs are modest next to the ones New Mexico and Connecticut use, so a wider band of middle-income Rhode Island retirees ends up owing something. A household combining a public pension or regular retirement-account withdrawals with monthly benefits can clear the limit on a fairly ordinary income.
 Past the threshold, the taxable share carries over from the federal return. Rhode Island begins with federal adjusted gross income, which already contains whatever portion of benefits the IRS counts, and then applies its own modifications. The state runs three income tax brackets, and its top rate sits below the top rates in Vermont and Connecticut.
 A separate modification covers a limited amount of pension and annuity income under a comparable age and income test. Retirees who clear the bar for one usually clear it for the other.
 Cost of living carries more weight than the tax rule for many retirees. Property taxes run above the national median, and housing in the Providence metro area, Newport and the South County shoreline costs more than in much of the country. Because the exemption threshold moves with inflation, anyone sitting near the cutoff should check the figure published for the filing year rather than relying on last year's number.
 Utah offsets Social Security tax with a credit, not an exemption 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Utah leaves Social Security inside taxable income and then returns the money through a tax credit rather than exempting the benefits outright. Retirees under the state's income cutoffs can erase the liability through the Social Security benefits tax credit, but only if they claim it on the return.
 The mechanics matter. Utah begins with federal taxable income, so whatever share of a retiree's benefits the IRS counts carries onto the state return. The credit then offsets the tax owed on that amount. It is nonrefundable, so it can reduce a bill to zero but cannot pay out more than the filer owes. The credit also shrinks as modified adjusted gross income rises past state-set thresholds. A retiree drawing a pension or taking large required minimum distributions alongside Social Security may qualify for only part of it, or none at all.
 For a filer with little other income, a full credit and a full exemption land in the same place. The difference shows up in the paperwork. Benefits sit in taxable income on the face of the return, with the credit applied further down, so the saving appears only when that line is filled in.
 The surrounding tax code is unusually simple. Utah applies a single flat rate to nearly all income instead of graduated brackets, and lawmakers have trimmed that rate several times in recent years. The Social Security credit is one of the few income-tested breaks inside an otherwise uniform system.
 Retirees weighing the whole picture will find Utah's effective property tax rate below the national average, which cushions the cost of taxing benefits at all. The state has also pulled in new residents along the Wasatch Front, the corridor running from Ogden through Salt Lake City to Provo. Home prices there have climbed steeply, and that increase can swamp whatever the credit returns.
 Vermont has the lowest exemption thresholds of the 8 states 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Vermont sets the tightest income limits of any state still taxing Social Security in 2026. Single filers with adjusted gross income below $50,000 and joint filers below $65,000 owe no state tax on their benefits. Above those cutoffs, the exemption narrows instead of vanishing all at once.
 The exemption itself is relatively new. Vermont created it in 2018; before that, benefits taxed at the federal level flowed into state taxable income with no carve-out for retirees. The phase-out was written to avoid a cliff. A couple reporting $70,000 in adjusted gross income does not suddenly owe tax on the full benefit the way they would under a hard cutoff. The exempt share shrinks as income rises through the phase-out range, and only retirees well past it see the entire benefit folded into taxable income.
 Connecticut's full exemption starts $25,000 higher for single filers, and New Mexico's sits $50,000 higher. A middle-income Vermont household — two modest pensions, a 401(k) drawdown and two monthly checks — is more likely to owe something than a household with identical finances in most of the other seven states.
 Vermont's income tax runs on graduated brackets, and its top rate is among the higher ones in the country. Retirement income beyond Social Security is generally taxable, though the state carves out partial exemptions for some government pension income, including certain military retirement pay and benefits paid under the Civil Service Retirement System.
 Property taxes add to the picture. Vermont's rank near the top nationally, and the statewide education property tax applies whether or not a household has children in school. Homestead property tax credits are available to income-qualified residents and can soften that cost for retirees living on fixed income.
 Housing costs diverge sharply inside the state. Chittenden County and the Burlington area carry the highest prices, while the Northeast Kingdom and other rural counties stay substantially cheaper. Where a retiree settles in Vermont can move the annual budget more than the tax treatment of benefits does.
